La jeune entrepreneuse Mariana Martin, f: Young entrepreneur Mariana Martin, founder of Carlota Boulangerie Mexicaine, talks about her migration journey.
L’immigration « privilégiée » – celle de: “Privileged” immigration – that of people who arrive by plane, have a profession or a trade, have some savings and speak two languages ─ as I did myself 10 years ago, is not always as easy as it seems at first glance.
Préjugés, étiquettes, difficultés, peurs: Prejudice, labels, hardship, fears, disillusionment and loss come with these journeys.
Mais parfois, à force de volonté et de t: But sometimes, through determination and hard work, some people manage to overcome these obstacles and plant a seed that eventually sprouts.
C’est cette histoire que j’ai voulu raco: That is the story I wanted to tell by sharing this account of the experience of Mariana Martin, a young entrepreneur who brought the sweetest flavours of Mexico in her luggage. She created a reassuring workplace for other Latin American women and a meeting point with the culinary traditions of her home country.
Ce fut un plaisir de discuter avec cette: It was a pleasure to talk with this curious, intelligent and sensitive young woman and to trace her journey, which, I hope, will inspire other women to start their own businesses.
<strong>La jeune entrepreneuse Mariana M: Young entrepreneur Mariana Martin, founder of Carlota Boulangerie Mexicaine, talks about her migration journey. She looks back on the difficulties she met along the way, which she overcame with the support of various communities.
En franchissant la porte de la boulanger: Walking through the door of Carlota bakery, you are transported to another world. An orderly, colourful universe. A group of women seem to be enjoying their work. They chat in Spanish. This world smells wonderful, and you leave with a bag of flavours.
Mariana Martin est une jeune femme souri: Mariana Martin is a smiling young woman who pays great attention to detail. Her contagious energy shows in how she dresses: leggings and a sports T-shirt, her long hair tied back in a ponytail. You can also see it in her gaze: her eyes are attentive and lively.
Pour Mariana, la nourriture est bien plu: For Mariana, food is much more than the fuel we consume. As far back as she can remember, she has always seen cooking as an act of love. “I like to think that I put a little bit of myself into every loaf of bread,” she confides.
Cette boulangère de 28 ans, née à Mexico: The 28-year-old baker, born in Mexico City, arrived in Montréal in 2017, after studying at the Culinary Institute in New York and at the Institut supérieur d’agriculture et d’agroalimentaire Rhône-Alpes in Lyon, France. She was only 15 when she realized she didn’t want to follow the path her family had laid out for her: becoming a lawyer.
« Ç’a été un choc pour eux, se souvient-: “It was a shock for them,” she recalls. “My boyfriend at the time, who is now my husband, motivated me.” Convincing her parents, especially her father Roberto, that she could be happy and earn a decent living in a kitchen was not going to be easy, any more than the road to the bakery was.
Au cours de ses premières expériences de: During her first work experiences in kitchens, Mariana was sexually harassed. “I was very disappointed to realize what awaited me: I was going to be seen as easy prey, simply because I was very young and I was a woman.”
À 18 ans, elle commence à étudier à New: At 18, she began studying in New York and working in restaurants.
Deux ans plus tard, en rentrant au Mexiq: Two years later, when she returned to Mexico, Mariana wanted nothing more to do with kitchens run by men. “I had heard of chef Elena Reygadas – named ‘World’s Best Female Chef’ in 2023 – whose businesses included the Rosetta bakery. I went to work with her. She was a great source of inspiration.”
Malheureusement, là encore, l’histoire s: Unfortunately, history repeated itself. Mariana was harassed again. The incident reached the ears of Ms<sup>.</sup> Reygadas, who reacted immediately: “This is a situation I will not tolerate in my spaces! I want every woman who works in my kitchens to feel safe. That person has been fired,” the chef assured her.
Cet épisode a marqué Mariana. « C’était: That episode left its mark on Mariana. “It was the first time I felt supported by another woman on an issue like that. I told myself that if I ever offered workspaces, it would have to be with the same perspective.”
En 2017, Mariana se rend à Lyon pour pré: In 2017, Mariana went to Lyon to study for a diploma in agri-food. There she met a woman from Montréal who had the dream – and the money – to build a bakery. “She offered to take the steps to bring me over on a work visa,” she explains.
Cet été-là, Mariana déménage à Montréal: That summer, Mariana moved to Montréal with her husband. At the end of the year, she started working at the bakery Farine et Vanille, on Parc Avenue.
À ce moment précis de son récit, Mariana: At this point in her story, Mariana pauses and brings up the concept of the “cultural iceberg.” According to it, when we come into contact with a culture we know only superficially, most of the elements that truly define it, and especially the most complex ones, escape us.
« C’est ce qui m’est arrivé lorsque je s: “That’s what happened to me when I got here. First I discovered the snow, the language, things I loved. But as I spent more time here, I started to see the prejudice against Latinos, the Eurocentrism, and how the colour of my skin would determine my role in this society.”
En novembre 2017, la jeune boulangère se: In November 2017, the young baker started making international pastries, focusing on French-tradition preparations. Then she felt the pull of her roots. “I realized there was a good opportunity to offer very high-quality Mexican bread, taking care with the ingredients,” she continues.
Les <em>conchas</em> à la vanille que Ma: The vanilla conchas Mariana began offering became very popular. Word of mouth did its work, first among Mexicans, then among Latinos as a whole. Little by little, Mariana drew more and more customers with her breads.
Mais les choses se sont compliquées. « L: But things got complicated. “The person who brought me to Montréal to work didn’t want to continue the business anymore. And at the time, I had a closed work permit.” She was left with two options: find someone else willing to employ her and handle her paperwork, or go back to Mexico.
Ne sachant que faire, Mariana s’est adre: Not knowing what to do, Mariana turned to a Mexican entrepreneur, Claudia Vega, a customer who ran Café 92 degrés. “Don’t go back to Mexico, you can’t leave us without your bread! I’ll sign the papers for you,” she assured her.
C’est ainsi que Mariana a commencé à tra: That is how Mariana started working at this café and, thanks to the support of Ms<sup>.</sup> Vega, launched her project: Carlota. “I worked 40 hours a week at the café, and in my free time, I made my bread and sold it,” she says.
Deux années de travail acharné ont suivi: Two years of relentless work followed, with gradual growth, like dough rising, until Mariana and her husband obtained permanent resident status. From there, she was able to spread her wings.
Lorsque Mariana et ses pains ont dépassé: When Mariana and her breads outgrew the capacity of Claudia’s kitchen, her father offered her financial help. “Oye hija, you’re very talented. Let me help you with your bakery,” he slipped in. Mariana hesitated at first, then ended up accepting. Four months later, in May 2022, Mr. Roberto died.
« Mon père n’a jamais pu la voir, mais p: “My father never got to see it, but for me, this business carries a lot of symbolism,” Mariana explains. So she rented a space, bought used equipment and kept filling her orders until Carlota bakery opened on Saint-Urbain Street on May 20, 2023. An important date: “It was the first anniversary of my father’s death,” she reveals.
Entre les murs et les fours de la boulan: Within the walls and ovens of Carlota bakery, there are several love stories that inspired its name: Mariana’s love for cooking and bread; her love for her father, who came to understand the value of her work. And then there is the story of Mariana and her husband, the boyfriend who supported her when she was very young.

Bien qu’elle se voie comme une immigrée: Although she sees herself as a privileged immigrant who came to the country without fleeing a conflict, with a profession and two languages, Mariana has faced, over these eight years, discrimination ranging from condescension to outright insult.
Alors qu’elle travaillait dans la premiè: While she was working at the first bakery, a woman walked in before the store opened to ask for a baguette. Mariana asked her to wait. “Where are you from? That’s why your country is the way it is, because you’re lazy,” the customer replied.
Mariana évoque aussi ces photos d’elle d: Mariana also mentions photos of her at her business, taken for the Getty Images platform and used without her knowledge to promote Emploi-Québec services, accompanied by the text: “Just arrived? Our services are here to guide you.” “A lot of people think I’m in those photos because I’m known for my business, but it’s only because of the colour of my skin. My image was used in contexts where what stands out is my origins,” she says.
Ce n’est pas la seule étiquette qu’elle: It’s not the only label she has struggled to carry. In 2018, when she took part in the Best Baguette in Montréal competition, the person presenting the award declared: “A big thank you to all the bakers who took part and to their wives who let them do this work.” She was the only woman competing.
« Bien que le machisme nous ait appris q: “Even though machismo taught us that a woman’s place is in the kitchen, from a professional standpoint, it’s not a place designed for us,” she notes.
Aujourd’hui, dans sa cuisine, où tout le: Today, in her kitchen, where everyone is an immigrant, a customer will sometimes comment in astonishment: “Look, they’re all women!” “If we were men, no one would say anything,” she notes. As an entrepreneur, Mariana is proud to offer “the safe, harassment-free workplace I wish I’d had when I was starting out.”
Au-delà des étiquettes, Mariana est opti: Beyond the labels, Mariana is optimistic about the future of Montréal’s Latin American community. But she also admits to being a little afraid. “I’d like to think that here in Canada, the political discourse about immigrants is nothing more than something prefabricated to win followers, and that our actions carry more weight,” she says.
Pour elle, tout repose sur la capacité d: For her, everything rests on communities’ ability to support one another, a solidarity like the one she herself benefited from when all seemed lost. “I’m convinced that we will keep looking out for one another and breaking the stereotypes of these racist discourses. Continuing to support and help each other is the best act of rebellion,” she says.
Mariana compte sur la nourriture pour êt: Mariana is counting on food to be the best tool of this resistance. “It’s a way to create empathy and break down prejudice, because we all love to eat. Through what we eat, we can talk about social and cultural crises, about globalization, about all the things we don’t usually think about that lie behind every dish we enjoy.”
